name: Gathering

origin.note: Suzuki and Yamashita gave an algorithm "moving the robots to a single point in finite steps" and showed that two oblivious robots cannot meet in SSYNC.

axes.name: Number of robots
axes.origin: Suzuki and Yamashita [Suzuki1999Formation] showed that two oblivious robots cannot gather deterministically in SSYNC, although the task is trivial in FSYNC; rendezvous thus became the first separator between the two schedulers [Flocchini2023Asynchrony] [Heriban2018Optimally]. For $n \ge 3$ robots the situation differs: with multiplicity detection, oblivious disoriented robots gather from any configuration even in ASYNC [Cieliebak2012Gathering], because a multiplicity point, once formed, can be kept unique and serve as the target [Bandettini2011Survey]. As Flocchini, Santoro, Viglietta and Yamashita put it, "Rendezvous is very different from the Gathering problem of having $k \geqslant 3$ robots meet" [Flocchini2016Constant] (their $k$ is $n$ here). Two robots cannot create such an asymmetry, so the two-robot case became the test bed for each new capability: unreliable compasses [Izumi2012TwoRobots], persistent memory [Suzuki1999Formation], lights [Viglietta2013Rendezvous] [Heriban2018Optimally] [Okumura2023External], and finite-state or finite-communication robots [Flocchini2016Constant]. The catalogue therefore splits gathering by team size: any $n \ge 2$, exactly two (rendezvous), and $n \ge 3$.

derived_from.relation: Gathering is $k$-grouping with $k = 1$, a single group of all $n$ robots, that is, point formation: the pattern consisting of one point of multiplicity $n$ [Flocchini2017Uniform] [Flocchini2026Universal]. General pattern formation algorithms usually exclude it, because multiplicity points need detection [Bramas2016Probabilistic].

summary: Robots must meet at a single point that is not fixed in advance, and stay there.
statement: $n$ robots start at distinct points and must all reach the same point in finite time and remain there. For $n = 2$ the problem is called rendezvous. **Time** is counted in rounds (FSYNC, SSYNC) or in epochs (ASYNC: intervals in which every robot completes at least one full Look–Compute–Move cycle); **colours** count light colours.

primer.intro: Imagine robots scattered over a field that must all meet at one spot, although nobody has said where. There are $n$ **robots**, points in the plane at distinct places; their positions form the **configuration**. Each robot repeats a **Look–Compute–Move cycle**: it takes a **snapshot** of where the other robots are (Look), decides on a destination point (Compute) and moves towards it (Move). They are identical, silent and **oblivious** (they remember nothing from one cycle to the next), and each uses its own **local coordinate system** (origin, axes, unit of length and handedness), so they agree on no direction. An adversary, the **scheduler**, decides the **activation** of robots, that is, when each performs a cycle: in SSYNC time runs in **rounds** and in each round it activates some of the robots; in ASYNC every phase may take any finite time. The robots must all reach the same point in finite time and stay there (for $n = 2$ this is called rendezvous). In the standard version $n \ge 3$, the scheduler is ASYNC, and robots have **weak multiplicity detection**: they can tell whether a point holds one robot or several (a **multiplicity**), but not how many.

ideas.title: Create one multiplicity, then every robot walks to it
ideas.idea:
1. If exactly one point is a multiplicity, walk straight to it.
2. Otherwise, look at the shape of the configuration and choose a point that every robot identifies in the same way despite their different local coordinate systems (for example the centre of a symmetric configuration), and move so that exactly one multiplicity appears.
3. From then on every robot follows rule 1, along paths that never create a second multiplicity.
ideas.analysis: A multiplicity is a landmark that no local coordinate system can hide: it looks special to every robot. Step 2 is the hard part, because the robots agree on no direction and the scheduler may stop a robot partway; Cieliebak, Flocchini, Prencipe and Santoro solve it with a case analysis of configuration types and gather $n \ge 3$ robots in ASYNC from every initial configuration [Cieliebak2012Gathering], the catalogue's introductory and current best result for this setting. In their algorithm a robot first checks for a single multiplicity; otherwise it checks for one symmetric shape (biangular) and moves to its centre; otherwise the robots elect some of themselves from the angles they form around the centre of the smallest enclosing circle: a single elected robot walks onto another robot, and several elected robots walk to the centre. Collisions anywhere else are avoided. Time is not analysed.
ideas.why_it_matters: It shows how a tiny sensing ability, telling one robot from several, makes an unsolvable problem solvable.

ideas.title: Two oblivious robots cannot meet in SSYNC
ideas.idea:
Take two robots, $A$ and $B$, and look at the round in which they would finally meet.

(a) If both moved in that round, the scheduler could have activated only one: it lands where the other was heading, not where the other is, so they miss.

(b) If only $A$ moved and landed on $B$, the scheduler could have activated both; unless $B$'s rule tells it to stay put, $B$ moves away and they miss again.

So meeting needs a situation in which, when both are activated, one robot jumps onto the other while the other stays. (c) But the robots are identical and agree on no direction, so the adversary can give them local coordinate systems in which each sees the other at the same spot, say one unit to its east. Identical robots with identical snapshots make the same choice: both stay or both move. The lopsided situation never occurs, and they never meet.
ideas.analysis: Suzuki and Yamashita proved this as Theorem 3.1 of [Suzuki1999Formation], even for robots with common handedness whose moves always reach their destination, so it also holds without these advantages. Natural rules fail in instructive ways: \"move to the midpoint\" brings the robots closer forever, but the scheduler activates one robot at a time so they never coincide; \"move to the other robot\" makes them swap places forever when both are activated. Extra power fixes this: with lights that both robots see, two colours suffice even in ASYNC [Heriban2018Optimally].
ideas.why_it_matters: It is the founding impossibility of the field: the scheduler keeps identical robots symmetric, and most later assumptions (multiplicity detection, lights, compasses) are ways to break that symmetry.

ideas.title: Without multiplicity detection, a multiplicity looks like one robot
ideas.idea: Suppose the robots stand on only two points, say $n-1$ robots on $p$ and one robot on $q$. A robot that cannot detect multiplicities sees just two occupied points, exactly what it would see if there were only two robots. The robots are thrown back into the two-robot situation above, and the scheduler, by activating only some of the robots on a point, can move groups around so that they never all stand together. Prencipe shows that against any algorithm the scheduler can first drive the robots into such special configurations and then keep them from ever gathering; the full proof is a longer case analysis.
ideas.analysis: The result holds for deterministic oblivious robots without multiplicity detection, for every $n \ge 2$, in SSYNC and ASYNC [Prencipe2007Impossibility]. In the fully synchronous model, by contrast, gathering needs no multiplicity detection [Flocchini2026Universal], and in ASYNC weak multiplicity detection is enough [Cieliebak2012Gathering].
ideas.why_it_matters: It explains why weak multiplicity detection became the standard assumption for gathering.

ideas.title: Short sight but a common compass: drift right, then down
ideas.idea:
Now each robot sees only the robots within distance $V$ (its **visibility radius**), but all robots agree on north and east (a **common compass**).

1. If you see a robot to your left, or above you on your own vertical line, do nothing.
2. If you see robots only below you on your vertical line, move down towards the nearest one.
3. If you see robots only to your right, move horizontally to the vertical line of the nearest one.
4. If you see robots both below you and to your right, make a diagonal move right and down, chosen so that you lose sight of nobody.
ideas.analysis: Robots only move right or down and never beyond the rightmost vertical line that holds a robot in the initial configuration, so they collect on that line and then at its lowest occupied point; the delicate part of the proof is that nobody is left behind out of sight. Flocchini, Prencipe, Santoro and Widmayer prove that this gathers ASYNC robots with non-rigid moves (Theorem 4.2 of [Flocchini2005Limited]), provided the initial configuration is connected (robots joined when at most $V$ apart); a disconnected initial configuration cannot be gathered at all. With rigid moves, a common compass gathers the robots at a point in time linear in the initial diameter, which is optimal; with agreement on one axis only, the same time brings them onto a horizontal segment of length 1, not to a point [Poudel2021TimeOptimal].
ideas.why_it_matters: It shows how a shared direction can replace global vision: robots that see little can still agree where to go.

glossary.definition: a computing entity modelled as a point of the plane (a unit disc for fat robots); all robots run the same algorithm
the positions of all $n$ robots at one instant, a multiset of points of the plane

one activation of a robot: in Look it takes a snapshot, in Compute it determines a destination point from that snapshot alone (and its own light, where lights exist), in Move it travels towards that point
the configuration as a robot observes it in Look (with the colours of the lights it sees, where lights exist), expressed in its local coordinate system
a robot keeps no memory from one Look–Compute–Move cycle to the next: Compute uses only the current snapshot

the origin, axes, unit of length and handedness in which a robot expresses its snapshot and its destination; robots agree on none of these unless the setting assumes chirality, one common axis or a common compass

the adversary that decides when each robot is activated: FSYNC activates every robot in every round, SSYNC a nonempty subset of the robots in each round, the sequential scheduler exactly one robot per round, and ASYNC lets each phase of each cycle take any finite time; every robot is activated infinitely often
the scheduler's choice to let a robot perform one Look–Compute–Move cycle; a robot that is not activated stays still
one time step of FSYNC, SSYNC or the sequential scheduler: each activated robot performs one complete Look–Compute–Move cycle
an interval of an ASYNC execution in which every robot completes at least one full Look–Compute–Move cycle; a bound of $X$ epochs holds for every division of the execution into consecutive epochs
a point of the plane occupied by two or more robots
the capability of a robot to see, for each occupied point, whether it holds one robot or more than one, but not how many
agreement of all robots on the direction and orientation of both axes of their local coordinate systems (north and east), not on unit or origin
the distance $V$ within which a robot sees other robots under limited visibility

history: Gathering started with an impossibility: two oblivious robots cannot meet in SSYNC [Suzuki1999Formation]. The community's main question became **the weakest set of capabilities that makes gathering solvable**: multiplicity detection [Cieliebak2012Gathering], a compass under limited visibility [Flocchini2005Limited], lights for two robots [Das2016Lights] [Flocchini2016Constant] [Heriban2018Optimally], and how many faulty robots can be tolerated [Agmon2006Fault] [Pattanayak2019Crash]. Running time (rounds, epochs) became a measure mainly for limited visibility [Degener2011Tight] [Castenow2022Unifying].

measures.name: Time
measures.description: rounds (FSYNC, SSYNC) or epochs (ASYNC) until the task is done; "finite" when only solvability is known

measures.name: Colours
measures.description: colours of the light per robot (0 for oblivious robots)

variants.title: ASYNC with weak multiplicity detection
variants.summary: With weak multiplicity detection, $n \ge 3$ oblivious, disoriented, asynchronous robots gather from any initial configuration.

results.note: Introductory and current best: solvable "for any $n > 2$ and any initial configuration", with non-rigid moves and weak multiplicity detection (a robot sees "none, one, or more than one" robot at a point). Theorem 5.36 covers $n \ge 5$; for $n = 3, 4$ the paper relies on earlier work of Cieliebak and Prencipe (SIROCCO 2002).

time.note: No epoch bound is recorded.

open: How many epochs does oblivious ASYNC gathering with weak multiplicity detection need?
variants.notes: Gathering is point formation, the pattern of a single point with multiplicity $n$ [Flocchini2017Uniform]. Under sequential schedulers, weak multiplicity detection is necessary and sufficient for gathering, and under FSYNC no multiplicity detection is needed [Flocchini2026Universal].

variants.title: Byzantine faults, SSYNC
variants.summary: Three robots with one Byzantine robot can neither gather nor converge in SSYNC.

variants.notes: Checked against the full text of [Flocchini2005Limited] (TCS 2005; preliminary version STACS 2001): robots are oblivious, anonymous, fully asynchronous (ASYNC), with non-rigid moves that cover at least a distance $\delta_r > 0$, no multiplicity detection, and "orientation": agreement on the directions and orientations of both axes, but not on the unit distance or the origin. The authors conclude that "with respect to gathering, orientation is at least as powerful as instantaneous movements". With rigid moves added (setting *Limited visibility with a compass, rigid, ASYNC*), Poudel and Sharma gather the robots at a point in $O(\Delta_0)$ epochs, which is optimal (Theorem 3 of [Poudel2021TimeOptimal], visibility radius $V = \sqrt{10}$).

variants.summary: With one common axis and rigid moves, asynchronous robots with limited visibility reach a horizontal segment of length 1 in time linear in the initial diameter; gathering at a point is not shown.

preconditions: $\Delta_0$ = Euclidean diameter of the initial configuration

results.note: Introductory and current best (Theorem 1): a relaxed gathering, all robots on a horizontal segment of length 1 not fixed in advance, in $O(\Delta_0)$ epochs; robots that occupy one point are not merged. FSYNC $O(g)$, $g$ the diameter (in hops) of the initial visibility graph, was known before.
assumes: two robots are joined when each lies in the axis-aligned $2 \times 2$ square centred at the other; the initial graph is connected

time.note: $\Theta(\Delta_0)$ epochs for the relaxed task (a segment of length 1); no bound is recorded for gathering at a point with one common axis.

open: Can asynchronous robots with one common axis and limited visibility gather at a point, and in $O(\Delta_0)$ epochs? [Poudel2021TimeOptimal] reach only a horizontal segment of length 1, because two robots on a horizontal line, disagreeing on east and west, may swap places forever.
variants.notes: Checked against the full text of [Poudel2021TimeOptimal] (Information 2021). The variant was previously recorded without rigid moves and as gathering at a point; the paper assumes rigid moves and proves only relaxed gathering for one common axis (Definition 3, Theorem 1). With a common compass the same algorithm gathers at a point in $O(\Delta_0)$ epochs (Theorem 3), (setting *Limited visibility with a compass, rigid, ASYNC*).

Every $\lambda$-contracting protocol, including Go-To-The-Center; works in two and three dimensions.

variants.summary: With lights and chirality, $n \ge 3$ robots gather in ASYNC with non-rigid moves and no multiplicity detection using 3 colours; whether 2 suffice is open.

preconditions: inherited: one colour is an oblivious robot

results.note: Concluding remarks: the SSYNC algorithm through the $5c$-colour simulation of a $c$-colour algorithm [Das2016Lights].
Theorem 6; 6 colours by a new $3c$-colour simulation (for a $c$-colour algorithm) of unfair SSYNC (Theorem 4). The authors conjecture that 3 is optimal.

time.note: Time is not analysed; only solvability.

open: Is 3 the minimum number of colours for ASYNC gathering with lights, and can chirality be dropped [Nakai2021Asynchronous]?
Self-stabilizing gathering of $n$ robots with lights [Heriban2018Optimally].

variants.title: Gathering, external light (FCOM), SSYNC, rigid
variants.summary: With external lights, $n \ge 3$ robots gather in rigid SSYNC with 3 colours, which is optimal; 2 suffice if a robot sees who shares its point.

preconditions: Theorem 2(1)
without seeing the robots at its own point

results.note: Introductory and current best (Theorem 6). With local awareness 2 colours suffice (Theorem 7), and local awareness cannot be dropped (Theorem 2(2) of [Otaka2026TwoState]).

time.note: Time is not analysed; only solvability.

open: Gathering with external lights in ASYNC [Otaka2026TwoState].

variants.title: Gathering, internal light (FSTA), SSYNC, non-rigid
variants.summary: With internal lights, 2 colours gather $n \ge 3$ robots in SSYNC only from restricted starts; 2 colours do not suffice in general, and whether more do is open.

preconditions: Theorem 1: 2 colours are impossible without restrictions on the start

results.note: Theorem 8, from starts in which robots are at most $2\delta$ apart.
Theorem 3: far fewer excluded starts; the remaining exclusions cannot all be removed (Theorem 2(3)).

time.note: Time is not analysed; only solvability.

colours.note: Unconditional gathering with more colours is open.

open: Gathering with internal lights in SSYNC from every start, with more than 2 colours, and in ASYNC [Otaka2026TwoState].

variants.title: Gathering, external light, sequential scheduler
variants.summary: If one robot moves per round, 2 external colours gather $n \ge 3$ robots, self-stabilizing, without chirality; oblivious robots cannot.

preconditions: oblivious robots cannot gather under this scheduler

results.note: Introductory and current best (Theorem 9); non-rigid moves. With internal lights and a round-robin scheduler, 2 colours suffice with rigid moves (Theorem 10).

time.note: Time is not analysed; only solvability.

variants.notes: Checked against the full text.

variants.title: Fat robots, few robots, no common orientation
variants.statement: Fat robots (unit discs) cannot share a point: gathering asks for a connected configuration of touching discs in which every robot sees all others.
variants.summary: Three and four oblivious fat robots, which block each other's view and motion, gather in ASYNC without any common orientation.

results.note: Introductory and current best for few robots: Theorem 3.1 ($n=3$) and the four-robot algorithm of Section 4.

open: Gathering any number of fat robots without chirality [Agathangelou2013Fat].
variants.notes: Checked against the full text of [Czyzowicz2009Fat] (TCS 2009; OPODIS 2006). Model: closed unit discs, identical and anonymous, oblivious, silent, no common coordinate system (but a common unit, the radius), ASYNC. A robot sees another if some segment between their boundary circles meets no third robot; a robot that touches another stops and ends its cycle; the adversary may stop a move after a distance $\delta$ unknown to the robots. Gathering means a connected union of discs in which every robot sees all others. The authors could not generalise to more robots ("We were unable to do it").

variants.title: Fat robots, chirality, any number
variants.statement: Gathering is Definition 1 of [Agathangelou2013Fat]: a connected configuration (every disc tangent to another), fully visible (every robot sees all others) and terminal, with all centres on the convex hull.
variants.summary: With chirality and known $n$, any number of opaque fat robots gather in ASYNC with non-rigid moves.

assumes: the radius is the common unit of distance
results.note: Introductory for any $n$ and current best (Theorem 26).

time.note: Time is not analysed.

variants.notes: Checked against the full text (arXiv 1209.3904).

variants.title: Transparent fat robots, no chirality
variants.statement: Transparent fat robots do not block sight but block movement. Gathering asks for a layered pattern around the centre of the smallest enclosing circle, with a unique robot at the centre [GanChaudhuri2015Leader].
variants.summary: Transparent fat robots without chirality gather into a layered pattern from every start whose robots can be ordered, which is exactly the asymmetric starts.

results.note: A short paper with no main theorem: an algorithm for $n \ge 5$ asynchronous oblivious transparent fat robots that gathers them "if no symmetric configuration [is] encountered during run time"; excluding such configurations is left open.

assumes: robots start separated (no two discs touching)
results.note: A configuration can be ordered, and a leader elected, if and only if it is asymmetric (Theorem 6); the algorithm gathers from every orderable start.

open: Gathering transparent fat robots from symmetric starts; the paper proves no general impossibility [GanChaudhuri2015Leader].
variants.notes: Gathering at a given point with limited visibility (dense packing around the point) is a different goal; it is studied by Cord-Landwehr et al. (SOFSEM 2011) and Sharma et al. (TAAS 2017), not yet read. Checked against the full texts of [GanChaudhuri2015Leader] (arXiv 1208.4484) and [GanChaudhuri2010Transparent].

figure.caption: Gathering: anonymous oblivious robots at distinct points of the plane must meet at one point, not fixed in advance, and stay there. Shown: the strategy of [Cieliebak2012Gathering] with weak multiplicity detection, in SSYNC rounds (ringed robots are activated; a move may stop early). In a symmetric configuration every robot computes the same centre; once a single multiplicity exists, every robot walks to it.

A multiplicity forms; all walk to it
